title: Server-owned network endpoint lifecycle across both interfaces
status: repaired and proven on the public successor candidate

root_cause.interface_asymmetry: The compatibility delete path released the server's auto-created endpoint inline in `crates/o3k-api/src/compute.rs`; the native canonical delete path (`bins/o3kd/src/native_adapters/resource.rs` -> `ComputeService::delete_server_for_auth_canonical`) had no endpoint cleanup at all.
root_cause.non_blocking_delete: The rc.23 native DELETE returned `{"complete": false}` (a non-terminal canonical operation), so convergence completed later through the agent/reconciler path, which also released nothing. A terminal-only cleanup inside the native adapter alone would not have fired.
root_cause.create_failure_preservation: The compatibility create-failure path preserved a request-owned endpoint whenever the durable server row referenced it, so a terminally failed create kept an ACTIVE endpoint next to its ERROR resource (issue #1034 defect 2).
root_cause.ordering_constraint: The endpoint release deletes the durable endpoint, while the fabric teardown plan (`NetworkBindingProjector::unbind_port`) reads that endpoint (address, MAC, realm) to compile its plan. Releasing before the terminal unbind would skip the host fabric teardown, so release must follow the unbind, per endpoint.

accepted_design.decision: synchronous + idempotent release on the normal mutation path; reconciler cleanup remains defence-in-depth (PP.5 follow-up)
accepted_design.ownership_rule: o3k-network centralises the discriminator: `is_server_owned_endpoint_name` / `server_owned_endpoint_context` accept only `o3k-server:<addressed-project>:<non-empty context>`, and `NetworkService::cleanup_server_owned_ports_for_project` releases only those, treats an absent endpoint as idempotent success, and fails closed on unexpected store errors.
accepted_design.release_seat: The terminal-success delete projection in `o3k-compute` (`project_terminal_binding_outcome`) releases each endpoint immediately after that endpoint's successful unbind, so every driver of convergence — request path, agent terminal-update consumer, periodic lifecycle sweep, poll surface — produces the same durable state for an accepted (202) and a synchronous delete.
accepted_design.retry_seat: `delete_server_with_accepted_operation`'s already-deleted shortcut releases from the durable create intent and reports the outcome, so replaying the same delete finishes a release that failed transiently.
accepted_design.create_disposition: `ComputeService::create_dependency_state_for_auth` derives `CreateDependencyDisposition` from durable canonical state: absent identity, DELETED, or ERROR with a terminally failed operation compensates; a live, in-flight, or inconclusive outcome (including UnknownOutcome) preserves the endpoint. The ERROR resource and the failed operation are retained as terminal evidence.
accepted_design.documented_deviation: issue #1034 comment: a release failure is reported (500) only where a request waits on it (request-path delete sites and the replay shortcut); when a background driver completes convergence, the failure is logged and retried by the next delete replay.

normative_anchor.clarification: Compensation section now states the endpoint ownership discriminator, that caller-supplied and foreign endpoints are preserved, and that release follows the terminal unbind and the terminal outcome rather than the observing request.
normative_anchor.public_api_change: none — no OpenStack/Keystone compatibility surface is added, removed, or re-scoped

regressions.unbind_before_release: crates/o3k-compute/src/lib.rs::create_and_delete_project_binding_outcomes_through_fake_provider (asserts the exact CreateOutcome, Unbind, Release sequence and the idempotent replay)
regressions.transient_release_retry: bins/o3kd/src/composition/pp4_endpoint_lifecycle.rs::transient_release_failure_is_reported_and_repaired_by_replay (injects one release failure at the collaborator boundary; the delete mutation fails, the replay finishes the release against the real NetworkService)

fail_before_fix_after.method: the shared cleanup helper and the disposition read were neutered (cleanup returned success without deleting; the disposition always returned Preserve) and the new suite was re-run against the otherwise-complete fix
fail_before_fix_after.result: 6 of 9 interface tests fail, including the exact rc.23 campaign symptom: `DELETE /v2.0/subnets/<id>` -> 409 "network operation is not allowed"
observed_failures: subnet_becomes_deletable_once_server_endpoints_are_released: subnet delete: {"error":{"code":409,"message":"network operation is not allowed"}}
terminal_create_failure_releases_the_endpoint_and_keeps_the_evidence: a terminally failed create left endpoints: [<uuid>]
fail_before_fix_after.discrimination: the three preservation guards (caller-supplied endpoint, foreign endpoint rejection, in-flight outcome) still pass with the fix neutered, because they assert that endpoints survive; they therefore discriminate behaviour rather than restating the implementation

campaign_harness.addition: after the cross-interface deletes, the durable `network_ports` rows named `o3k-server:%` must be empty (read-only sqlite read, evidence file `server-endpoints-after-deletes.json`), so the successor campaign asserts the repaired invariant directly rather than inferring it from the teardown

follow_up.pp5: crash window: process death after the canonical compute delete reaches terminal and before the cross-service endpoint release. Requires a bounded reconciler sweep that repairs orphaned server-owned endpoints of terminal-deleted servers. Not a substitute for the synchronous release; tracked for PP.5 hardening.

claims.proven: source-level repair with in-process, fail-before/fix-after evidence covering both reported defect classes and the safety cases
claims.not_proven: no other host or profile is covered; the PP.5 crash window remains open

campaign_proof.ubuntu: phase 9 asserts zero durable `o3k-server:%` endpoints after the cross-interface deletes; the compatibility-created server was deleted through the native interface whose canonical delete returned HTTP 202 complete=false, so the release ran from the terminal outcome; the caller-supplied endpoint survived
campaign_proof.debian: same assertion and the same 202 path on Debian 12
campaign_proof.verdict: both hosts PASS with Core manifest verdict PASS
